intro:
How we look at skin

Skin does not deteriorate overnight. Nor does it recover overnight.

Even for the same brown patch, pigment that sits in the epidermis (the outer layer) and pigment that has descended into the dermis (the deeper layer) are treated in completely different ways. Even for the same sagging, loss of elasticity in the skin itself and descent of the underlying tissue call for different methods. Even for the same pores, whether sebum or loss of firmness is the cause changes which procedure is chosen.

That is why, before listing procedure names, we start by establishing what is actually happening in your skin now.

And we add one more thing. We explain how long the procedure will last, how many sessions are needed, which side effects occur and how commonly, and what this procedure will not solve. We believe that narrowing the gap between expectation and result is what ultimately leads to satisfaction.

What makes this clinic different

A practice long engaged with cells and regeneration

This clinic has practised with regenerative medicine at its centre. We look not only at the lines and pigment on the surface but at what is happening to collagen and cells beneath them. So we ask "what should be restored?" before "what should be removed?".

We prefer what comes from your own body

We have long placed weight on the autologous approach — using material obtained from the patient themselves. The more a substance is brought in from outside, the more room there is for a foreign-body reaction or allergy; material from your own body leaves relatively less. Rather than putting in everything that can be put in, only what is truly needed, at a minimum.

We do not tell only the good part

Our explanations contain numbers you will not often see elsewhere. Skin booster injections cause bruising in roughly one person in three, and research shows that laser toning on its own returns the skin to its pre-treatment state after about six months. There is one reason we write down figures that look unhelpful — someone who knew in advance does not become anxious during recovery.

How a consultation runs

  1. ListeningWhat troubles you most, procedures you have had before and how you reacted to them, the medicines you take now, whether you are pregnant or breastfeeding, the conditions and allergies you live with. Please tell us even what seems trivial. One aspirin changes the size of a bruise, and one contraceptive pill changes the outcome of pigment treatment.
  2. Finding the causeThe same appearance can have different causes. We distinguish whether pigment sits shallow or deep, whether sagging is a matter of elasticity or of descent, whether pores are about sebum or about firmness. The type and order of procedures are decided at this stage.
  3. Plan and explanationWe set out the procedure we recommend, how many sessions and at what intervals, how long recovery takes, the side effects that can occur, and what this procedure will not solve. We proceed only once you fully understand and agree.
  4. Procedure and after-careAlong with soothing care afterwards, we explain what to do at home. We also agree how to reach us if anything is wrong, and when to come back.
Please tell us at the consultation
  • if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding
  • if you take aspirin or anticoagulants (blood thinners) — bruising can be extensive
  • if you take contraceptives or hormone preparations — these directly affect pigment conditions such as melasma
  • if you take acne medication (isotretinoin) or have recently stopped it
  • if you scar easily (keloid tendency)
  • if you get recurrent cold sores (herpes simplex) — laser procedures can bring them back, so we prescribe medication in advance
  • diabetes, autoimmune disease, immunosuppressants, or any condition in which wounds heal slowly
  • if there is currently inflammation, a wound or infection where the procedure would be done
  • any other skin procedure in the last three months (laser, filler, threads, injections — anything)
  • if you have ever had an allergic reaction to a filler, anaesthetic or antibiotic

From one week before the procedure, please avoid strong exfoliation and excessive sun exposure, including tanning. On tanned skin the risk of side effects from laser procedures rises considerably, and the procedure may have to be postponed.

tags.d:
In three lines
  • An exosome is the "parcel" one cell sends to another. Signalling substances are inside it.
  • Cell and animal studies are promising, but research in humans is still at an early stage.
  • We use them topically only, alongside a procedure that opens the skin barrier.

A signal sent from cell to cell. The cells of the body exchange signals with one another. An exosome is the very small vesicle that carries such a signal. It is about a thousandth the thickness of a hair, and inside it are various kinds of RNA, proteins and lipids.

Put simply

If a cell is a factory, an exosome is a parcel passed between factories. Inside the parcel are work orders such as "make more collagen" or "reduce inflammation". What has been established so far, however, is only that "there are orders inside the parcel"; how much effect that parcel has when placed into human skin is still being confirmed.

How it is carried out

Exosome-based products are applied to the skin. As they are poorly absorbed when simply applied, it is usual to use them together with a procedure that creates microchannels in the skin surface with fine needles, or immediately after fractional laser.

We will be honest with you
  • Exosomes make theoretical sense, but they are at a stage where they have not yet been sufficiently verified in humans.
  • There is no clinical study directly comparing them with existing procedures, so there is as yet no basis for saying "one is better than the other".
  • No exosome product has yet been approved in Korea as a medicine or a medical device. We do not hide this fact from you.
Points to be aware of
  • Redness, swelling and flaking from the accompanying procedure can last several days.
  • Avoid sun for 48 hours after the procedure and use sunscreen.

In three lines
  • Tightening what has loosened (ultrasound, radiofrequency) and lifting what has descended (threads) are different things.
  • Ultrasound and radiofrequency work gradually. It takes about three months to become clear.
  • Thread lifting reports swelling in 34% and bruising in 26% within four weeks. Allow time in your schedule.

Lift what has descended, or tighten what has loosened? Facial ageing does not come from a single cause. Lifting therefore varies by what the problem actually is. If the elasticity of the skin itself has fallen, methods that use heat to make collagen again are right; if tissue has descended, physically lifting and fixing it is right.

Put simply

Think of a stretched jumper. If the fabric itself has gone slack, it needs pressing (ultrasound, radiofrequency) to tighten the weave. But if the whole garment has slipped off the shoulder, no amount of pressing will help — it has to be lifted back onto the shoulder and held there (thread lifting). In most people the two are mixed, so the first question is which is the greater cause.

By method
  • Ultrasound lifting (HIFU) — ultrasound converges on a point at a set depth and creates small thermal coagulation points, which the body then refills with new collagen. The effect appears not immediately but over months, becoming clear from around day 90.
  • Radiofrequency lifting (RF) — heat is delivered broadly across the dermis. If ultrasound works on "points", radiofrequency is closer to working on a "plane". Studies report relatively low pain, and firming is felt from around week four.
  • Thread lifting — barbs on the thread catch and lift descended tissue, and the stimulus the thread creates rouses the cells that make collagen. Smooth threads without barbs have almost no lifting power.
This may suit you if
  • the jawline has lost definition and looseness under the chin and on the neck concerns you
  • the cheeks have descended and nasolabial folds have deepened
  • you do not want surgery and would prefer gradual change
Cases to think again about
  • Where laxity is already advanced — research shows the effect falls as sagging becomes more severe, so non-surgical lifting alone is unlikely to meet your expectations.
  • Where skin is very thin with little subcutaneous tissue — threads may show or be palpable.
  • If you take aspirin or anticoagulants — bleeding and bruising increase.
  • If you have a metal implant or pacemaker, are pregnant, or have an infection in the area to be treated.
Honestly, about how long it lasts
  • Ultrasound — in research, the improvement at day 90 continued to one year. There are, however, no data beyond one year.
  • Radiofrequency — studies observed up to six months. Beyond that has not been established.
  • Thread lifting — maintenance up to 18–24 months has been reported, but there are no data beyond two years.
  • There is as yet no good study directly comparing the three methods, so we do not assert that any one is "the most effective".

※ Possible side effects — ultrasound and radiofrequency: temporary redness, swelling and heat; rarely altered sensation or burns. Thread lifting: swelling, bruising and pain within four weeks, and subsequently palpable threads, skin dimpling and infection have been reported. We explain in detail at the consultation.

In three lines
  • Not every brown patch is the same. Melasma, freckles, seborrhoeic keratosis and post-inflammatory marks differ in both cause and treatment.
  • Treatment that is good for one kind of pigment makes another worse. That is why diagnosis comes before any procedure.
  • Something that looks like a seborrhoeic keratosis can be skin cancer. An examination is needed before treatment.
Put simply

It is like a stain on clothing. A stain on the surface (epidermal pigment) wipes off with a light clean, but one that has soaked into the lining (dermal pigment) needs many washes. And if it is not a stain at all but a knot in the thread (a seborrhoeic keratosis), no amount of washing helps — it has to be cut away. The difficulty is that all three look much the same shade of brown from outside.

Telling pigment apart
WhatFeaturesDirection of treatment
MelasmaAcquired, symmetrical on both sides. Darker in summer, lighter in winterSun protection above all. Topical and oral medication are the basis; laser is an adjunct
FrecklesConstitutional predisposition. Usually under 3 mmResponds relatively well to pigment lasers
Seborrhoeic keratosisA benign growth of the epidermis (raised to the touch). Does not disappear on its ownNot a pigment laser but removal (cryotherapy, shaving, laser, electrocautery)
Blemishes and lentiginesFlat brown patches in sun-exposed areasSkin cancer must be ruled out before treatment
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentationCaused by earlier inflammation — acne, a wound, a procedureTreat the inflammation that caused it first. A procedure can make it worse
Melasma — the order matters
  • 1. Sun protection. Without thorough protection from sunlight, no melasma treatment can be expected to work.
  • 2. Topical medication. This is the standard treatment. Visible change takes time.
  • 3. Oral medication. There are ingredients with established effect, but side effects are possible, so we prescribe only after consultation.
  • 4. Laser. An adjunct. There is evidence that results are better when combined with the treatments above.
Keratoses and blemishes — examination comes first

What looks like a seborrhoeic keratosis can in fact be skin cancer or actinic keratosis. We always examine and differentiate before treating a blemish, and where appearance alone is not enough we perform a biopsy.

Pores — starting from the cause

There are three main reasons pores look large: excess sebum (sebum control is needed alongside), loss of firmness (collagen stimulation is needed), and enlarged follicles. Several causes overlap, so treatment must differ from person to person.

※ There is no established evidence that pores can be permanently reduced. Making them less noticeable through care is the realistic goal, and we say so in advance.

In three lines
  • Laser toning is many gentle passes rather than one strong one.
  • It is not the first treatment for melasma but the third. It holds only alongside topical and oral medication.
  • Having it too often can leave white spots, which do not readily reverse. That is why we keep to a two-week interval.

Not once hard, but many times gently. Laser toning delivers laser at low power, over a wide area, repeatedly. The aim is to target the pigment granules alone, without destroying cells, and to lower pigment-producing activity.

Put simply

If a strong pigment laser is a hammer blow, laser toning is closer to rubbing many times with sandpaper. A hammer is good on a hard stain but puts a hole through a thin wall. Sandpaper, though, strips the colour if you rub the same place too often. That is why the interval matters.

The figures as they are
  • Laser toning is not first-line treatment for melasma but a measure used alongside others when topical treatment is not working.
  • Analysis of the research shows that with toning alone, the skin returns to its pre-treatment state after about six months. Where it was combined with sun protection and topical medication, the effect was maintained.
  • We therefore do not recommend laser toning on its own.
The side effect that matters most — white spots

Having it too often and too much can cause loss of colour in small white spots (punctate hypopigmentation). Research shows a clear relationship with the number of sessions, and this side effect responds poorly to treatment and can persist for years.

Our rules
  • As a rule the interval is two weeks or more. We do not offer "intensive care once or twice a week".
  • We plan a total of 8 to 12 sessions and adjust as we watch the response.
  • At every visit we check pigment change and any sign of white spots developing, and stop immediately if they appear.
  • Please use sunscreen after the procedure, and restart topical medication one to two days later.

In three lines
  • If a filler fills, a skin booster changes the quality of the skin.
  • Research confirms improvement in hydration, elasticity, texture and radiance, but no study has yet looked at long-term outcomes.
  • Contrary to the belief that a "cocktail" of many ingredients is better, results have shown a single ingredient to be more marked.

Not filling, but changing the quality of the skin. Where a filler shapes by filling a hollow, a skin booster is injected in small amounts at many points within the skin to improve the skin's own hydration, elasticity, texture and radiance.

Put simply

Think of a leather bag. A filler is like putting contents inside to give it shape; a skin booster is like feeding oil into the leather itself to make it soft and lustrous. The shape stays the same, but the material changes.

How many sessions?
  • Where the change is modest — a difference can be felt after one session.
  • Where ageing change is marked — three sessions at monthly intervals are generally recommended.
  • Maintenance afterwards — every four to six months.
Recovery and side effects
  • Bruising, swelling and tenderness are common and usually settle within two weeks.
  • Small nodules are uncommon but can occur.
  • The thin skin around the eyes and the bridge of the nose need particular care.
We will be honest with you

Most studies to date are small, and none has reported long-term treatment outcomes. We therefore do not promise a duration categorically. We adjust the plan as we watch the response.

In three lines
  • A substance that holds water is injected into the skin in very small amounts at many points.
  • Roughly one person in three bruises, and it settles in about six days on average. Allow time in your schedule.
  • The duration confirmed in clinical trials is up to three months after the last session.

Hydration from within the skin. Hyaluronic acid is injected into the skin (the dermis) in very small amounts at many points. Hyaluronic acid has the property of drawing in and holding a large quantity of water by itself.

Put simply

Think of watering a dry pot plant. Spraying water on the surface (cosmetics) dries quickly. This injection is closer to mixing water-retaining granules into the soil. The granules do break down in time, however, so it is not permanent.

Recovery — in figures
  • In clinical trials, bruising occurred in 35.7% — roughly one person in three.
  • Swelling and small wheal-like bumps can appear alongside.
  • All were mild or moderate and resolved within six days on average.
  • If you have an important occasion — a wedding, a presentation, an interview — allow at least one to two weeks.
Changes confirmed in research

In a controlled clinical trial, an elasticity index improved by about 10% at three months, and skin thickness and complexion radiance improved. The duration confirmed in that study, however, was up to three months after the final injection; beyond that has not been established.

Points to be aware of
  • Three sessions at monthly intervals is the basis, with maintenance every four to six months afterwards.
  • Avoid alcohol and tobacco after the procedure, and do not massage or press the treated area hard. Avoid saunas and steam rooms too.
  • Rarely, injection procedures carry vascular risk. We explain this fully at the consultation.

In three lines
  • The names sound similar, but the ingredients and actions are entirely different. Rejuran is salmon DNA; Juvelook is a synthetic polymer.
  • Rejuran is about skin quality; Juvelook is about volume and firmness.
  • Juvelook does not dissolve with the enzyme used to dissolve fillers. "If I don't like it, I can just dissolve it" does not apply.

Similar names, entirely different substances. The question is not which is the better product, but which your skin needs now.

Put simply

Rejuran is closer to fertilising a field: it improves the soil itself so that plants grow well. Juvelook is closer to putting a stake in the field: the body builds collagen around that stake, and volume appears. The difficulty is that once a stake is in, it is not easily pulled out.

Comparison
RejuranJuvelook
Main ingredientPolynucleotide (PN) — long DNA fragments obtained from salmonPDLLA (synthetic polymer) microparticles + hyaluronic acid
Expected changeSkin quality — texture, hydration, fine lines, firmnessVolume and firmness
Main side effectsPain on injection, redness and swelling for one to three days, short-lived lumpsLate-onset nodules and inflammatory nodules — can appear weeks or months later
Reversible?—Does not dissolve with hyaluronidase, the enzyme used for fillers
How Rejuran is given
  • Three to four sessions initially at two- to four-week intervals, then periodic maintenance
  • The effect begins at four to eight weeks and develops over three to six months
  • Injection is on the painful side. We reduce this with anaesthetic cream and other means.
Juvelook — a side effect needing particular care
  • If the material gathers in one place it can form a nodule, so the practitioner's skill in spreading it evenly at the right depth matters.
  • Areas with thin skin, such as under the eyes, need careful selection.
  • Because Juvelook does not dissolve with the enzyme used for fillers, the decision must be made carefully from the start. We explain this clearly before the procedure.

In three lines
  • Different products are used for different areas. Where a firm product is right differs from where a soft one is needed.
  • The most important risk is vascular occlusion. It is rare, but serious complications are reported.
  • If pain suddenly worsens, the skin turns pale, or vision blurs, tell us immediately.

The more a procedure fills, the more where and how much matter. Hyaluronic acid is a substance that occurs naturally in our skin, cartilage and joint fluid. The character of a filler is determined by how firm it is. The firmer it is, the more support it gives, but it is unsuited to fine, superficial work where the skin is thin. So the accurate way to put it is not "this filler is the best" but "this product is right for this area".

The risk you must know about — vascular occlusion

If filler enters a blood vessel by mistake, serious complications including tissue necrosis, visual disturbance up to blindness, and stroke have been reported. It is rare, but knowing about it allows a fast response.

If, during or immediately after injection, there is sudden severe pain, visual disturbance, or the skin turns pale and blanched, tell us at once.

How we are set up to respond
  • We identify a safe plane, taking into account that major vessels run slightly differently in each person.
  • As a rule we use a blunt-tipped cannula and inject slowly at low pressure.
  • At any sign of a problem we stop immediately and carry out the standard management set out in international guidelines.
  • Where there are visual symptoms, we arrange immediate ophthalmology referral.
Points to be aware of

In a Korean study, 74.6% of patients treated for filler complications had been injected by someone who was not a medical practitioner. Always have this done at a medical institution, with an approved product.

Semi-permanent makeup — taking back the five minutes you spend every day

Semi-permanent makeup places pigment in a shallow layer of the skin to hold the shape and colour of brows, eyeliner or lips for a period of time. The pigment fades gradually, so periodic touch-ups are needed.

Here it is performed at a medical institution by a medical practitioner, who checks skin condition and allergy history beforehand and follows infection-control standards.

What you must know
  • An allergic reaction to the pigment can occur anywhere from immediately after the procedure to years later. It is most common with reds, but possible with any colour.
  • Redness and swelling immediately afterwards are almost inevitable and usually settle over two to three weeks.
  • Always tell the radiographer before an MRI, and say so at once if you feel burning during the scan.
  • Pigment spreading or changing colour over time is genuinely common. Decide the design carefully.
Tattoo removal — erasing takes longer than marking

Laser tattoo removal is a medical act and may be performed only by a medical practitioner at a medical institution. The number of sessions varies greatly with the colour and type of pigment, the depth at which it was placed and how long ago, and several treatments are needed.

※ If the tattooed area has ever itched, swollen or developed a rash, tell us at the consultation without fail. Laser treatment is in some cases not recommended for a tattoo that has caused an allergic reaction.

In three lines
  • It briefly interrupts the signal to the muscles that create expression, smoothing the lines they make.
  • The effect begins at two to three days, peaks at one to two weeks, and lasts three to six months.
  • Repeating at intervals shorter than three months can lead to resistance. Keeping the interval matters.

For lines made by expression, there is a way of managing the expression. Botulinum toxin acts at the point where the signal to move a muscle is transmitted, relaxing the muscle. The effect is not permanent, and the muscle returns to its original state in time.

Put simply

Think of a line as the crease left by folding paper. Folding the same place over and over deepens the crease. Botulinum toxin stops that place being folded for a while — it buys the paper time to flatten out.

How the effect runs
Effect begins2–3 days after injection
Peak effect1–2 weeks after
DurationAbout 3–6 months per session
Procedure time10–30 minutes
Resistance — the more often you have it, the less it may work

Repeated injection can lead the body to produce antibodies and the effect to decline. The greatest risk factor is repeating at intervals shorter than three months. We therefore use the smallest dose that achieves the desired effect, keep to a minimum three-month interval, and look into the possibility of resistance if intervals are shortening or the dose keeps rising.

Points to be aware of
  • Temporary weakness at and around the injection site, bruising, swelling and, rarely, eyelid droop can occur, and usually recover within a few weeks.
  • It must not be given during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or where there is neuromuscular disease. We always check this at the consultation.

outro:
How to get on after a procedure

WhenWhat
On the dayAvoid saunas, steam rooms, strenuous exercise, alcohol and tobacco. Do not rub or press the treated area. Wash gently with lukewarm water.
1–3 daysRedness, swelling, bruising and stinging can occur and mostly settle on their own. Cold compresses help. Restart make-up as advised by your medical team.
1 weekAvoid saunas and swimming pools, and strong exfoliating or peeling products.
Every daySunscreen daily from the day after the procedure. Sun during recovery is the most common reason pigment is left behind.
Contact us straight away if
  • pain becomes steadily worse with time
  • the treated area turns pale and white, or becomes mottled in a net-like pattern
  • vision is blurred or the eye hurts
  • you develop a fever, or pus forms
  • redness and swelling do not reduce after several days and instead increase

The sooner you tell us, the easier it is to deal with.

About sun protection

Treating pigment is bailing out water; sun protection is turning off the tap. However much you bail with the tap left open, the water does not go down.

  • The SPF on a product refers to protection against UVB, and PA (+/++/+++) to UVA. Check both.
  • SPF 15 or above for daily life; SPF 30 or above for outdoor activity.
  • Most people apply too little and so do not get the protection stated. Apply a generous amount, spreading it in two passes.
  • Apply 20 to 30 minutes before going out, and reapply every two to three hours.
  • Ultraviolet light reaches you on cloudy days too. Do not make an exception for season or weather.
  • Melasma and pigment marks are also affected by visible light. In such cases tinted or tone-up formulations containing iron oxide help.

Frequently asked questions

How long does the effect last?
It varies greatly with the type of procedure, your skin, your age and, above all, daily habits (sun, smoking, sleep). We have written the ranges reported in research into each procedure's description. But those are averages, not promises. We set out the likely course for you individually at the consultation.
Is one session enough?
It depends on the procedure. Some produce a felt change after one session; others only become meaningful once the planned number is completed. For pigment and regenerative procedures in particular, keeping to the intervals and the plan matters for both result and safety. Rushing raises the risk of side effects.
Can I have several procedures together?
Some combinations help one another, and some must be separated by an interval. Performing procedures that use heat or energy on the same area one after another raises the risk. We set the order and intervals at your consultation.
Can I go back to normal life straight away?
In most cases yes, on the same day, but redness, swelling and bruising can remain for a few days. If you have an important occasion, allow at least one to two weeks.
I am worried about side effects.
Every medical procedure carries the possibility of side effects. We explain the ones that can occur without omission and obtain your consent before proceeding, and we tell you how to reach us immediately if something is wrong. Please raise anything that worries you at the consultation.
